Our approach involves incorporating the abstract theory of spaces of representations, defined using functors that map the groupoid to the category of matrices, combined with the concrete representation of the groupoid's underlying topological space.

A molecular core, referred to as DR21C, located within the infrared dark nebula, the Dragon, has been found to possess a protostar that is in the process of forming a massive star. This discovery was made possible by low-frequency submillimeter observations capable of penetrating dense regions and revealing temperature and density information. Further investigation used mid-to-high-frequency submillimeter observations which provided a detailed picture of the core, revealing a temperature and density gradient. A calculation of the core's and surrounding envelope's masses yielded results of approximately 13 to 20 solar masses and 13 to 30 solar masses respectively. Driven by the presence of a massive protostar and guided by theoretical models, researchers concluded that the core, with a mass of 43 solar masses, had transitioned from an envelope-dominated state to a core-dominated state, indicative of a critical juncture in its evolution.

Let $\T$ be a triangulation of the sphere and $\U\subset\T$ a subset of edges, with $|\U|$ evolving from $3$ to $n+2$. We investigate harmonic polynomial fields defined on the edges of $\U$ and study how fields on $\U$ can be determined from those on a subfield with fewer edges. We aim to establish a one-step recurrence formula to compute the harmonic polynomial field on $\U$ for any given field on a subfield with fewer edges. This process should be efficient enough to provide a solution for fields on up to $n+2$ edges within the order of $n$ computations.

The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface tension and
crystalline ordering within the bulk. However, even when both factors are negligible,
 fluids like soap foams exhibit unexpected friction properties depending on their structural
 features, specifically the angle of their grains. A unified framework is introduced
 that explains how the granular structure impacts friction through gradient energy,
 applicable to a range of packings from random to highly ordered configurations.

This study involves creating a multi-classifier network to accurately classify skin cancer images. A critical aspect of this research is identifying appropriate training data, as it is essential to exclude images that are likely incorrect or mislabeled from the training set in order to achieve optimal results in outlier detection using the K-Nearest Neighbors method and validation sets. A total of 130 images were flagged as suspect in the dataset provided. As part of this project, we conducted an outlier detection analysis using the K-Nearest Neighbors method and validation sets. Furthermore, we conducted an experiment to evaluate the effect of training with suspect images on model performance. Our findings show that using all available images to train the model leads to a decrease in accuracy, while using only images considered reliable results in higher accuracy. Additionally, we investigated the effect of training with suspect images on model performance and our findings indicate that there is a significant drop in accuracy when training with suspect images.

The interaction between a rotating interface and an invading liquid is governed by a balance of forces, torque, and shear stress. When the interface is curved, as in a spherical or cylindrical cell, this interplay results in a complex pattern of liquid fingers with varied spacing. Using high-speed cameras to study spinning cells of various shapes and sizes, we have observed non-uniform finger formation and cell-specific scaling relationships that reflect the interplay of balancing forces and curved surface characteristics. These relationships demonstrate that the curvature of the cell enhances the stability of the interface, leading to larger fingers at the cell's inner edge. Similarly, in a cell with a constricted neck, the pattern of invasion is affected by the neck's curvature, and can switch from a stable, single-finger state to an unstable, bifurcated state as the neck's radius is decreased. High-resolution simulations of this scenario also exist, but to our knowledge, this is the first experimental evidence of its kind.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules, E-CCHCD and N-CND, emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with estimated abundances of (1.0±0.3)×10^10 per molecule and (0.5±0.2)×10^10 per molecule, respectively. A possible third component, E-CND, was also detected but is less certain. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene molecules were detected using the ATLAS survey and further analyzed using the SIMBA and GUMSOFI telescopes. In neural machine translation, the attention model's effectiveness has been questioned, given that the target vocabulary significantly limits source-target alignments. This study introduces a novel look-forward attention mechanism that enhances the standard attention by incorporating source-target alignments. We explored three variants of our mechanism and found that they consistently boost the performance of base neural machine translation models. Furthermore, our method complemented the strengths of both neural machine translation and convolutional neural network-based attention models, resulting in improved scores. We also analyzed the attention patterns and confirmed that our mechanism properly captures target-producing information.

The widespread adoption of grid computing was hinderly dependent on its successful translation into usable technology for everyday applications, thereby creating a feedback loop that drove the field's development. Through the study of grid computing's history, we identify a distinct category of technological advancements that were driven by a desire to make complex computer technology more accessible to a broader audience. A particular framework, known as the Interoperable Heterogeneous Workflows framework, serves as a microcosm for understanding the interplay between technological innovation and the need for interconnectivity, as well as the role of user experience in driving both grid and complex computer technologies forward.

A unified dark sector model, known as the Combined Dark Fluid model, has been proposed to explain the current rapid universe expansion. This model involves two dark fluids with different temperatures and densities, one of which is a dissipative component. By applying this model to the early universe, we find that it's capable of reproducing the 2.725 K cosmic microwave background temperature and accounting for the large-scale structure formation. Furthermore, it complies with the standard big bang nucleosynthesis results. This model also experiences a phase transition at a critical point, which may correlate with the observed universe acceleration phase.

Our research examines the importance of the J/ψ decay mode J/ψ → (γ + missing energy) in relation to neutrino and dark energy, specifically dark matter, within the framework of low-energy effective field theories. By utilizing the (euclidean) Witten's approach to low-energy effective actions, we determined the J/ψ decay mode's imaginary component in effective field theories containing neutrino and dark matter. Subsequent analysis revealed that the J/ψ invisible decay mode's imaginary component is nonexistent when starting from a conformally invariant neutrino sector. Conversely, the J/ψ invisible decay mode's imaginary component does exist in the dark matter sector, with estimated corrections to J/ψ invisible decay width ranging from 0.3 to 10 times the typical width, depending on dark matter's mass and coupling strength. Additionally, our study demonstrated that the J/ψ invisible decay mode's visible component, resulting from dark matter particles annihilating into light particles, can be significantly affected by strong binding effects and condensation, which could potentially influence the decay width by a factor of twenty.

This study introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) which is a innovative method for multivariate functional time series. We achieved this innovation by adapting the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) technique, originally designed for individual time series, to accommodate multivariate data. Our research further expands on existing work by altering the optimal matching algorithm used to determine the order of multivariate time series, and we developed the multivariate cost function framework specifically for this purpose. Additionally, we conducted a simulation study to evaluate the performance of MFSSA and compared it to the existing method, RE-DINA. Our results showed that MFSSA yields superior outcomes. Moreover, we applied MFSSA to real-world data, specifically examining temperature anomalies across different latitude bands and it helped us identify distinct patterns within different latitude domains.

This research examines a random walk that takes place within a limited domain $D$ for an indefinite amount of time, where the walk starts at point $x_0$ and has a known probability distribution $P_x$ for each point $x$ within the domain. The goal is to investigate how likely it is that the walk will spend a significantly long period of time, say $s$, within a particular area $A$ of the domain $D$ for any given point $x$ within the domain. This probability can be denoted as $\Psi_x(s)$, and we aim to establish general conditions under which the probability distribution $\Psi_x(s)$ persists for all points $x$ within the domain $D$ for an infinite period of time. This entails that the probability of the walk spending an extremely long period of time, say $s$, within the area $A$ of the domain $D$ remains nonzero for all points $x$ within the domain $D$ for an infinite period of time. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck/IPP in Germany features a plasma generator with a helical antenna to evaluate high-power RF plasma interaction. A review is provided of previous studies on plasma characteristics and the validation of the helicon mode of the plasma generator. Plasma parameters were determined using a Langmuir probe system, verified by particle flux measurements, and the effectiveness of the helicon mode in creating a stable plasma sheath was confirmed. Additionally, the paper offers an overview of the plasma generator's design and its operation in helicon mode, detailing how magnetic field patterns influence plasma formation. Furthermore, results are presented from localized particle flux measurements, confirming previous findings on plasma parameters, and analyzing flux profiles to determine plasma drift velocities.

While artificial intelligence has made significant progress in automatic cell segmentation, fully-automated software for clinical use has not been established due to difficulties in detecting all cells and accurately defining the boundary of individual cells. A new approach called W-Net has been developed to achieve precise cell segmentation by finding all nuclei first and then fusing them using a convolutional layer. W-Net consists of two main components: a nucleus identification module and a fusion module. The nucleus identification module uses a conventional U-Net to locate all nuclei, outlining cells that are partially outlined and removing cell boundaries that are incorrectly defined. W-Net has been tested on real-world data sets and shows comparable performance to existing methods, outperforming them on average according to evaluation metrics.

Let's consider a finite field k with an odd characteristic and its algebraic closure K. Also, let G be either the special orthogonal group SO2n+1(Q) or the symplectic group Sp2n+2(Q) where n is a positive integer, and Q is a nonsingular algebraic matrix from the field k. The regional converse theorem for the absolute Galois group of k is true if there are two embeddings from the absolute Galois group of k to the automorphisms of G(F) that, for any given place F of K, agree on the rational functions of G(F). In our proof of the regional converse theorem for the odd special orthogonal and symplectic groups in positive characteristic, we use the Deligne--Rosen method of descent and the strong approximation property of the groups SO2n+1 and Sp2n+2. Additionally, our proof assumes that there aren't any subfields L of K that contain the algebraic closure of k and have a specific property determining the primes of which are disabled to contribute certain Galois modules, and the set of those disabled primes does not form a finite set.

In recent years, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have gained significant popularity, consistently achieving superior performance in complex data analysis tasks. However, due to the lack of clear fundamentals resulting from faulty Fourier transform properties, many researchers remain uncertain about the underlying principles of GCNNs. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by presenting four key concepts of GCNN's spectral convolution module, accompanied by a new Fourier transform-based methodology to simplify the convolution process. A novel approach, "node-wise matched filtering," involves matching individual nodes with reference signals to determine their characteristics. This method can be applied to both spatial and spectral GCNNs. A simplified framework for spectral convolution was also developed and compared to the original method to highlight the underlying principles of GCNNs. A new type of GCNN, called theta-filter GCNN (TF-GCNN), was then proposed by combining the matched filtering and periodic filtering methods. TF-GCNN outperformed existing GCNN models on multiple benchmark datasets.

In a theoretical framework with a scalar field, Einstein's gravity theory is modified to include a term derived from a Chern-Simons action for specific gauge groups. This modification leads to the emergence of black holes with hair in rotating situations, unlike in the general relativity case. By employing metric transformations and the Weyl transformation for the scalar field, a new frame is established where the scalar field's potential appears in a simplified form. This enables the description of non-rotating black holes and solitons based on their mass/charge ratios. The study focuses on grave solutions with positive specific gravities and excludes extreme or Kerr black hole solutions. The (effective) cosmological constant's and gauge field strength's impacts on solution types are also considered. The study reveals that for certain gauge groups, specific ratios of mass to charge correspond to soliton rather than black hole solutions. The process of forming these solutions is analyzed through perturbative and numerical methods. The study of black holes with hair also raises questions about the corresponding gauge field configurations. The process of solving for gauge field strengths involves solving a set of nonlinear differential equations. The study of rotating black holes with hair has not been extensively studied, unlike their non-rotating counterparts. The study of rotating black holes with hair has not been extensively studied, unlike their non-rotating counterparts.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the mechanical characteristics of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties, specifically lateral displacement, is crucial for distinguishing benign from malignant tissues but is often impeded by limited viewing angles in ultrasound elastography. This research introduces a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method to determine lateral tissue displacement across a specific area using data from a single measurement with a limited aperture. A realistic computer model simulating elastography measurements was used to validate the VOSA method, demonstrating its capability to recover precise displacement information even with a limited viewing angle. Compared to existing techniques, VOSA exhibited superior performance in estimating displacement across a broader range of viewing angles. Diverse simulation scenarios were employed to further evaluate VOSA, demonstrating its robustness in real-world applications. This research indicates that VOSA can be an highly effective and precise approach for determining tissue displacement in ultrasound elastography, particularly when there are restrictions on viewing angles.

We introduce a new framework called "Rational Pseudocode" to bridge the gap between mathematical proofs and programming examples shown in lectures. This approach aims to connect instructional code snippets, which are commonly observed in teaching, to more formal algorithm descriptions. We believe that by connecting these examples to structured algorithms, educators can generate more efficient teaching methods, and researchers can leverage them for tasks such as validating algorithms submitted for proofs-of-work. In addition, we provide a basic tool for converting algorithms to pseudocode, which can approximate the style of common programming languages.

In the one-dimensional $k$-means clustering problem, data points are arranged along a line, and points with the same label must adhere to a contiguous interval. This variation requires solving a root extraction of degree $k$, but with an allowable error $\epsilon$, this problem can be settled within $poly(1/\epsilon)$ dimension-independent rounds in the word RAM model using just two random accesses per round. This performance is surpassed by our new algorithm which employs multiple random accesses per round, specifically $O(\log^3 k)$ rounds, and our result for $d=1$ dimension is a special case of a more general outcome valid for $d$ dimensions, where the number of rounds scales as $O((\log k)^3 \cdot \log^2 d)$, although clustering accuracy is determined by the number of rounds in a different metric.

In multi-agent competitions like pursuit-evasion games, both participants compete against each other with opposing goals, where one seeks to capture the other, and vice versa. These games serve as a microcosm for exploring complex strategies and intelligent decision-making at scale. We have developed a novel way to categorize competition dynamics using self-organizing maps (SOM), specifically hierarchical divisions that capture the intricacies of these games. Our study involves a simple pursuit-evasion model where multiple agents move around a rectangular field, and we analyzed the outcomes of various simulation trials. Our key contribution involves applying these hierarchical divisions to understand the competitions' behavior, thereby providing a clear picture of how different strategy groups evolve over time. Our research utilized 49 different competitions, each consisting of 100 time steps, and we found that the SOM effectively grouped the data into 7 categories, each defined by distinct patterns of capture and evasion tactics employed by the competing agents. Our work paves the way for further research on these complex competitions, specifically exploring ways to incorporate additional variables, such as longer simulation trials, and our findings are readily available for download on the UCI machine learning repository.

This research focuses on developing an efficient method to determine the direction of vector bosons, specifically W and Z bosons, in high-energy muon collisions resulting from the decay of heavy particles such as top quarks. Our study addresses the significant challenge of identifying these directions when there are multiple muons produced, which can arise in future particle accelerator experiments with high-intensity collisions. Our approach, called VWFinder, utilizes advanced tracking techniques and sophisticated algorithms to accurately establish the origin of muon particles and consequently pinpoint the direction of the parent vector boson. Our computational simulations reveal that VWFinder can effectively identify the direction of vector bosons even in the most demanding scenarios with multiple muons, and our results demonstrate that this approach can effectively reduce estimation errors caused by limited resolution in experiments.

In complex real-world settings like robotics, agents typically perform multiple tasks simultaneously to achieve multiple goals, making model-based multi-task reinforcement learning a subject of significant interest (Bonsor et al., 2019; Erez et al., 2018; Merel et al., 2020). This approach involves using an environment model to forecast the outcomes of actions taken in a specific environment. Although using such models offers several advantages, they also come with significant computational costs, prompting researchers to capitalize on memory-based systems to limit the prediction expenses (Vidal et al., 2019; Kurckai-Cai et al., 2020). Our study focuses on examining the benefits of modular learning through memory-based systems in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning. We created an algorithm called Multi-Task Future Prediction Prevention (MTf4), a variant of the f4 method (Curtil et al., 2019), tailored for achieving multiple tasks. Through extensive simulations, we found MTf4 outperforms the f4 method in various scenarios, consistently demonstrating the benefits of modular learning through memory-based systems in multi-task reinforcement learning.

We are presenting a concise report on the events that transpired during the 1964 International Congress of Logic, Philosophy, and History of Natural Science held in Leipzig, East Germany. This convention was notable for having a notable absence of Western logicians, which significantly influenced the meeting's atmosphere. Despite this challenge, the conference managed to succeed in its objectives, thanks in large part to the dedication and effort of its participants. A gathering of prominent logicians, including Kurt Godel, Alonzo Church, and Hilary Putnam, did not occur as the paper had initially predicted. However, the author did get the opportunity to meet with Stephen Kleene, who provided valuable insights into the historical development of logic systems.
This study extends Hadamard's three spheres theorem to non-homogeneous second order elliptic differential operators in Clifford analysis.

In crisis situations like natural disasters or hostage situations, where multiple people are present and it's difficult to identify who is speaking, determining the speaker of each utterance can be very helpful for authorities to guide their response. However, identifying the speaker of each statement in such scenarios, known as speaker extraction or posterior extraction, is a challenging task due to background noise and overlapping speech from multiple speakers. We approach this problem as an inverse problem, applying the concept of an inverse problem to solve speaker extraction, where we use a generator model that produces a clean mix of speech given observations of multiple speakers. We evaluate our proposed method, a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, on two datasets - Convex and SIW Convex, derived from the Librispeech dataset, and find it outperforms existing methods in terms of PSNR and SSIM metrics.

This article examines invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from the perspective of symplectic geometry. We derive a necessary condition for invariant surfaces to exist, which is based on the Lie algebraic structure of the system's generator. Consequently, this condition can also be seen as a requirement for the system's stability properties. A comparative analysis is performed among various stability criteria, including their relationships and limitations.

The interstellar medium is home to complex structures that influence the behavior of radio waves as they travel through space, specifically affecting pulsar scintillation patterns. Pulsar B1133+16, located 800 parsecs from Earth, has a stable and bright signal allowing for detailed analysis of scintillation patterns, both in space and time. A thorough examination of time-series scintillation data from the LOFAR radio telescope over several years revealed that patterns of scintillation change at a rate of approximately 0.04 degrees per year, indicating that the major contributing factor to variations in scintillation patterns is not the Earth's motion, but rather the proper motion of the pulsar. Furthermore, patterns of scintillation indicate that the linear polarization of the pulsar is likely close to 100%. An investigation of time-series data also uncovered a time-dependent shift in scintillation patterns, which occurred about 10 years ago, and which is believed to result from a sudden change in the emission characteristics of the pulsar rather than a similar change in the interstellar medium. A statistical analysis of time-series data from the Big Dipper Pulsar also revealed similar properties of scintillation patterns. This study presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves realistic waveform generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of this model result in pitch control difficulties, primarily caused by unbounded output probabilities. To overcome this challenge, QPNet incorporates a pitch-aware convolution neural network with input parameters, ensuring the output probabilities remain bounded. The model demonstrates superior quality and control over traditional WaveNet through subjective evaluations and objective metrics. Furthermore, a compressed version of QPNet, CPNet, with comparable performance is also presented.

The bicategory of shadows, previously established in a prior study, is revealed to be equivalent to the bicategory of paths within a specific subcategory of the category of functors that preserve structure, specifically those functors mapping from the category of oriented surfaces to the category of oriented surfaces while ignoring surface Reidemeister moves. A key aspect of the (2,2)-category of shadows can be captured by examining properties of natural transformations, specifically the property of being invariant under ambient isotopy, which in turn is shown to be equivalent to the property of being invariant under surface Reidemeister moves. This leads to the conclusion that the (2,2)-category of shadows can be redefined as the (2,2)-category of functors mapping from the category of oriented surfaces to the category of oriented surfaces while being invariant under surface Reidemeister moves.

For individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, acquiring visual-gesture based information is extremely challenging, if not impossible, due to their limited access to auditory cues.  To better understand the difficulties such individuals face, this paper delves into analyzing a particularly demanding scenario in sound localization known as the "blind spot" - a 90 degree arc in front of them where they struggle to identify the source of sounds. Our research leverages a recently proposed real-time neural network for monaural sound source localization, and we report on an exploratory study of five profoundly deaf participants who learned American Sign Language (ASL) gestures for 20 common daily objects.  In a controlled, quiet environment, we safely exposed them to sounds from various angles, up to 60 degrees from their front, and asked them to identify the source of the sound in addition to the object it represented.  Our results show a significantly lower accuracy rate in sound source localization within the "blind spot" area, and it Correlates strongly with the difficulty of understanding the corresponding spoken word.

In recent years, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been widely applied to complex network analysis, despite primarily being designed for static simple graphs. GNNs typically rely on a Euclidean distance metric that can lead to inaccurate results for many real-world datasets involving large distances. We propose a novel weighted convolution layer that leverages the Koszulian distance, a more suitable alternative for many applications, especially those involving a clear direction or hierarchy. Furthermore, we introduce a new category of GNNs, Lorentzian Graph Neural Networks (L-GNNs), incorporating the Koszulian distance, and demonstrate its effectiveness on high-stakes real-world data, including brain connectivity and stock market networks, achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

This research focuses on an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be recovered using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate.

We present a novel exponential delay discounting model based on the Tsallis statistics framework, an alternative to the traditional exponential model popularized by Samuelson. Our model differentiates from the conventional exponential model in its risk-sensitive properties and potential neural correlates. We derive the optimal stopping policy for an intertemporal choice task and analyze its implications, including the effects of information gain on decision-making. Furthermore, we investigate the conditions under which the Tsallis model reduces to the exponential model, and the consequences of using the exponential model when the underlying distribution varies.

We outline the fundamental principles of gauge harmony within massive gravity theories, focusing on the Fierz-Pauli model as a starting point. A brief overview of the key challenges faced by these theories is provided, followed by an in-depth examination of the harmonic gauge issue in linearized gravity. We then systematically build the massive gravity models from a harmonic gauge perspective, beginning with the dS/lattice version, followed by the mmf model, the ghost-free, fully metric version, and finally the dRGT version. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these models for the harmonic gauge issue.

For a quantum system in thermal equilibrium, a representation of the canonical thermal expectations is developed using Weyl-Wigner transforms, based on a phase-space perspective. This representation leads to a new class of polynomial equations that systematically derive the expected outcomes for various system observables, thereby extending the classical Hamilton-Jacobi formalism to a quantum context. This approach is particularly useful for examining the properties of closed quantum systems in thermal equilibrium, as it bypasses the need to specify a temperature scale. The development of this theory is further illustrated by applying it to a model quadratic Hamiltonian and a bosonic Dicke model.

The notion of negative absolute temperature has been intellectually intriguing
scientists for nearly eight decades. Since the phenomenon's discovery in the
1940s, it has sparked both fascination and skepticism. This paper delves into the
historical context surrounding the concept's emergence and explores the
underlying mathematical structures that negative temperatures embody. We also
examine the optimistic implications of this structure on the coherence of the
Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics and the mathematical framework
of type of quantum theory known as Weyl quantum mechanics.

Within the most fundamental $\mathbb{Z}_2$ "scoto-seesaw" framework, where a dark sector is coupled to the dark sector's reflected image, we generate a minimal set of dark matter operators. This basic setup enables us to effectively treat the dark sector as a single, unified unit. By applying this framework to the weakly interacting massive particle (WIMP) scenario and the "electroweak scale" as a reference point, we find that the vacuum stability of the Higgs field is significantly improved when the dark sector's underlying physics is characterized by a mass hierarchy. Furthermore, this hierarchy leads to a more pronounced impact on the dark matter relic density in comparison to the leading $\mathcal{O}(1)$ couplings. Consequently, the "disfavored" logarithmic behavior of the WIMP relic density is suppressed, and this scenario becomes more in line with the observed value of the dark matter density in the universe.

We employ a one-band Hubbard model to study the strong-correlation effects of 4d and 5d $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ double-degenerate levels in cubic crystals. The model's results are compared to exact calculations for a small cluster with exchange coupling, yielding similar physical characteristics. The interplay between on-site and nearest-neighbor interactions becomes evident as we examine the phase diagrams of 4d and 5d materials. The one-band model can be modified to include spatial fluctuations of the electron filling, accurately replicating previous small-cluster, exact results. The one-band Hubbard model can be mapped to a Gutzwiller variational approach, with the wave function's overlap serving as an important factor in the phase diagrams' behavior. The variational approach also enables the calculation of material-specific $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ orbital hybridization and effective on-site and nearest-neighbor interactions. The one-band Hubbard model can be mapped to a strong-coupling expansion in the large-$U$ limit, resulting in an effective Peierls-Hubbard Hamiltonian with on-site and nearest-neighbor couplings. The one-band Hubbard model's predictions are compared to experimental data from X-ray scattering and optical conductivity for 4d and 5d materials, with the variational approach providing a means to calculate the orbital hybridization and effective couplings.

This study investigates modifications of singularities in higher-ranking topological quantum field theory. It classifies non-degenerate surface crossings that preserve topological invariants under specific algebraic changes, known as Frobenius closures. We demonstrate that all non-degenerate crossings, including those initially excluded, can be represented through commutative diagrams involving closed strings. This representation enables us to define closure operators that transform crossings into Frobenius closures. Notably, this process transforms certain types of crossings that were initially dismissed as irrelevant into relevant crossings, thereby expanding the collection of defined crossing types by an infinite set.

Utilizing raw chest X-ray images for modeling patient outcomes has shown limited success 
due to variations in image quality being misleadingly linked to clinical guidelines.
This paper presents an innovative approach that preprocesses images in accordance 
with recognized medical protocols, thereby bypassing this discrepancy. We introduced 
a novel, fully automated multi-modal image modification framework, inspired by 
clinical practices, to alter images in line with COVID-19 diagnosis protocols. 
This framework comprises three key components: removing patient identification 
information, redacting sensitive data, and obscuring findngs from related images; 
and a versatile image processing module to conform images to established clinical 
criteria. We assessed this framework on publicly accessible datasets containing 
COVID-19 and normal chest X-rays and discovered it effectively applied medical norms 
to images. To model patient outcomes, we used a pre-trained CNN and found that 
preprocessing images yielded more accurate predictions compared to using raw images.

ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional vector analysis. It enables users to visualize high-dimensional vector spaces, define their own measures, and apply non-linear reduction techniques to better understand their data. It also provides tools for identifying clusters, boundaries, and singularities within the data, as well as for conducting quality control and verifying model validity. Additionally, it can be used for dimensionality reduction, feature selection, and anomaly detection. With this tool, users can choose from several visualization methods, including self-organizing maps, kernel principal component analysis, and autoencoders, and it's particularly useful for interpreting artificial neural networks.
